<title>Décadas después del 11 de septiembre, el polvo tóxico y el trastorno de estrés postraumático podrían estar acelerando el envejecimiento cerebral entre los socorristas</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759201/original/file-20260831-50-fxel1p.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Las secuelas de los ataques al World Trade Center dejan una larga sombra sobre los sobrevivientes.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/firefighters-gather-by-the-south-reflecting-pool-during-the-news-photo/2234175241">Adam Gray/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Cientos de socorristas me han dicho que recuerdan exactamente cómo se sintieron durante los ataques al World Trade Center, incluso 25 años después.</p>

<p>Me cuentan que recuerdan no haber podido pensar, ver ni oler nada. Solo podían concentrarse en cavar y retirar los escombros del camino. No podían descansar porque quienes estaban atrapados bajo los escombros no podían esperar. La muerte los rodeaba por todos lados, y lo único que podían hacer era dar lo mejor de sí para contenerla.</p>

<p>Aunque lo que ocurrió el 11 de septiembre no tuvo precedentes, tragedias similares ocurren con bastante frecuencia. Como <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3axQJv8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">médico especialista en salud ocupacional</a> que trabaja con los rescatistas del 11 de septiembre, me resulta fácil imaginar que otros bomberos, paramédicos y trabajadores de la construcción pensaban lo mismo mientras intentaban salvar vidas tras los mortíferos terremotos del verano de 2026 en <a href="https://theconversation.com/earthquakes-in-venezuela-expose-a-severely-under-resourced-and-unprepared-healthcare-system-287003">Venezuela</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/colombia-earthquake-has-killed-at-least-132-my-research-helps-explain-why-it-was-so-destructive-289478">Colombia</a> e <a href="https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-earthquake-magnitude-77%20-c31ad3cf07fa83d2d443e8d85e5c9d84">Indonesia</a> o las desastrosas <a href="https://theconversation.com/nepals-flash-floods-show-the-devastating-power-of-cascading-hazards-290611">inundaciones en Nepal</a>.</p>

<p>Es posible que estos socorristas también tengan que recuperar restos humanos de entre los escombros. Estos momentos de profundo dolor están rodeados de polvo, gases tóxicos y gritos de auxilio. Y este trauma pasa factura.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Vista aérea de los escombros del World Trade Center, con multitudes de equipos de primera respuesta que intentan rescatar y sacar a los sobrevivientes de entre los escombros" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=402&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757075/original/file-20260831-50-be7gu1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=505&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">La destrucción del World Trade Center no tuvo precedentes, pero este tipo de desastres no son infrecuentes en todo el mundo.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/rescue-workers-sift-through-the-wreckage-of-the-world-trade-news-photo/1339510">Mario Tama/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Ya se trate de desastres industriales o nucleares, fenómenos climáticos extremos, incendios forestales, erupciones volcánicas, guerras o ataques terroristas, los equipos de primera respuesta y las comunidades afectadas pueden sufrir <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/s1049023x19000141">efectos significativos en su salud física y mental</a> tanto durante las operaciones de rescate y recuperación como durante los años posteriores. Todos son vulnerables a sufrir daños físicos y mentales, sin importar qué tan bien entrenados estén.</p>

<p>Las investigaciones de mi equipo sugieren que, entre estos riesgos, se encuentra el trastorno de estrés postraumático, que puede <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-025-03769-7">hacer que su cerebro envejezca más rápido</a>.</p>

<h2>El trastorno de estrés postraumático entre los socorristas</h2>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/acute-stress-and-early-signs-of-ptsd-are-common-in-firefighters-and-other-first-responders-heres-what-to-watch-out-for-247365">El trastorno de estrés postraumático, también conocido como TEPT</a>, es un trastorno de salud mental complejo que puede desarrollarse después de vivir o presenciar un evento traumático. <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-trauma-the-more-we-talk-about-it-the-more-it-means-279754">El trauma psicológico</a> se refiere a los efectos emocionales duraderos de la exposición directa o indirecta a circunstancias que ponen en peligro la vida o a la violencia.</p>

<p>El TEPT puede manifestarse con recuerdos intrusivos, evitación, estado de alerta elevado, problemas para dormir y cambios en el estado de ánimo y el pensamiento. La ansiedad y la depresión suelen presentarse junto con el TEPT.</p>

<p>Alrededor del 23 % de los socorristas del World Trade Center <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/s003329171100256x">han sido diagnosticados con TEPT</a>. En comparación, se estima que alrededor del 6 % de la población general de EE. UU. <a href="https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/essentials/epidemiology.asp">ha padecido TEPT</a> a lo largo de su vida.</p>

<p>Cuando hablo con los socorristas del 11 de septiembre, describen su TEPT y sus dificultades cognitivas como problemas interrelacionados que siguen afectando sus vidas hasta el día de hoy. Esos recuerdos traumáticos siguen siendo vívidos, y algunos socorristas continúan experimentando ansiedad, depresión, pensamientos intrusivos, problemas para dormir y dificultad para controlar sus emociones.</p>

<h2>El trauma acelera el envejecimiento cerebral</h2>

<p>A medida que envejecen, muchos de los socorristas del 11 de septiembre también han notado que su memoria, concentración y agudeza mental se deterioran. Cada vez les preocupa más perder su independencia. En lugar de presentarse como afecciones separadas, las enfermedades físicas, los cambios cognitivos y el malestar emocional <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jts.22631">a menudo se refuerzan entre sí</a>.</p>

<p>En otro estudio, investigadores de mi equipo monitorearon la función cognitiva de más de 5,000 socorristas del World Trade Center sin demencia entre 2014 y 2022. A lo largo de aproximadamente cinco años, 228 desarrollaron demencia antes de los 65 años. Los socorristas con la exposición más grave al <a href="https://doi.org/%2010.1038/s41582-021-00576-8">polvo y escombros potencialmente neurotóxicos en la zona cero</a> presentaron una <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.089161">incidencia de demencia</a> sustancialmente mayor que aquellos con exposición mínima o que utilizaron de manera constante equipo de protección personal, como respiradores. Esta relación se mantuvo después de controlar los factores demográficos, de estilo de vida, médicos y genéticos.</p>

<p>Antes de empezar a estudiar los efectos del 11 de septiembre en la salud, estaba investigando a trabajadores expuestos a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.shaw.2021.12.906">metales neurotóxicos y contaminación industrial</a> en el norte de Italia. Al conocer las toxinas dañinas presentes en el polvo del World Trade Center, comencé a preguntarme si los socorristas del 11 de septiembre podrían enfrentar riesgos similares a largo plazo para su cerebro. Esa preocupación se intensificó cuando las tomografías cerebrales de ambos grupos mostraron un <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/bs.ant.2022.%2005.002">aumento similar en los depósitos</a> de una proteína relacionada con la enfermedad de Alzheimer y el deterioro cognitivo llamada <a href="https://theconversation.com/alzheimers-disease-is-partly-genetic-studying-the-genes-that-delay-decline-in-some-may-lead-to-treatments-for-all-205914">beta-amiloide</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Persona que mira directamente a la cámara, con un casco de construcción adornado con varios parches, entre ellos uno con un grabado de las Torres Gemelas y la leyenda «NUNCA OLVIDEMOS»" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757073/original/file-20260831-50-fbqqek.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">CEl trabajador de la construcción James Nolan es uno de los socorristas del 11 de septiembre que enfermaron a causa del polvo tóxico y los escombros del World Trade Center.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Attacks%20Health%20Trials/9d835c4865764a72886f12a1859298d9/photo">AP Photo/David Goldman</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Una investigación de mi equipo también reveló que los cerebros de los hombres que participaron en las labores de rescate del 11 de septiembre y que padecían TEPT presentaban <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-025-03769-7">resultados de resonancia magnética que indicaban cerebros de mayor edad</a> en comparación con los que no padecían TEPT.</p>

<p>En ese estudio de 2025, medimos las estructuras cerebrales mediante resonancias magnéticas y un modelo de inteligencia artificial para estimar la edad cerebral de cada participante. El modelo de inteligencia artificial había sido entrenado para predecir la edad cronológica de una persona a partir de la estructura general de su cerebro, basándose en datos de más de 11 500 resonancias magnéticas cerebrales de personas sanas de entre 5 y 95 años. Utilizamos la diferencia entre la edad cerebral predicha de una persona y su edad real como medida del envejecimiento cerebral acelerado.</p>

<p>También observamos que los socorristas con TEPT tenían cerebros que parecían aproximadamente <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-025-03769-7">tres años más viejos</a> que su edad cronológica. Por el contrario, la edad cerebral estimada de los socorristas sin TEPT coincidía aproximadamente con su edad cronológica real. Cada mes adicional que un socorrista pasó trabajando en la Zona Cero se asoció con aproximadamente cuatro a cinco meses adicionales de envejecimiento cerebral aparente, lo que sugiere que el tiempo de exposición al desastre desempeñó un papel clave en este proceso de envejecimiento.</p>

<h2>Cuidado de los socorristas</h2>

<p>Las experiencias de los socorristas demuestran que los efectos del 11 de septiembre siguen siendo un problema de salud actual. Estas consecuencias para la salud evolucionan a medida que las personas envejecen, y siguen requiriendo apoyo coordinado en los ámbitos mental, cognitivo, físico y social décadas después.</p>

<p>Cada aniversario del 11 de septiembre trae de vuelta recuerdos vívidos de la tragedia, junto con la misma inquietud, frustración y dolor de haber estado allí. Sin embargo, muchos de los que estuvieron en primera línea me han dicho que sienten orgullo y un sentido de pertenencia al saber que ayudaron a personas que lo necesitaban desesperadamente. Su servicio sigue siendo un ejemplo perdurable de solidaridad humana en un momento de crisis.</p>

<p>Honrar ese legado también significa proteger a quienes acuden en nuestro auxilio durante una emergencia. Creo que, como sociedad, los estadounidenses tienen la responsabilidad de salvaguardar, proteger y cuidar su salud a lo largo de toda su vida. Ellos estuvieron ahí para Estados Unidos en uno de sus momentos más oscuros; los estadounidenses deben estar ahí para ellos en los años venideros.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291747/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Las secuelas de los ataques al World Trade Center dejan una larga sombra sobre los sobrevivientes
Adam Gray/Getty Images Cientos de socorristas me han dicho que recuerdan exactamente cómo se sintieron durante los ataques al World Trade Center, incluso 25 años después
Me cuentan que recuerdan no haber podido pensar, ver ni oler nada
Solo podían concentrarse en cavar y retirar los escombros del camino
No podían descansar porque quienes estaban atrapados bajo los escombros no podían esperar
La muerte los rodeaba por todos lados, y lo único que podían hacer era dar lo mejor de sí para contenerla
Aunque lo que ocurrió el 11 de septiembre no tuvo precedentes, tragedias similares ocurren con bastante frecuencia

Como médico especialista en salud ocupacional que trabaja con los rescatistas del 11 de septiembre, me resulta fácil imaginar que otros bomberos, paramédicos y trabajadores de la construcción pensaban lo mismo mientras intentaban salvar vidas tras los mortíferos terremotos del verano de 2026 en Venezuela , Colombia e Indonesia o las desastrosas inundaciones en Nepal
Es posible que estos socorristas también tengan que recuperar restos humanos de entre los escombros
Estos momentos de profundo dolor están rodeados de polvo, gases tóxicos y gritos de auxilio
La destrucción del World Trade Center no tuvo precedentes, pero este tipo de desastres no son infrecuentes en todo el mundo

Mario Tama/Getty Images Ya se trate de desastres industriales o nucleares, fenómenos climáticos extremos, incendios forestales, erupciones volcánicas, guerras o ataques terroristas, los equipos de primera respuesta y las comunidades afectadas pueden sufrir efectos significativos en su salud física y mental tanto durante las operaciones de rescate y recuperación como durante los años posteriores
Todos son vulnerables a sufrir daños físicos y mentales, sin importar qué tan bien entrenados estén
Las investigaciones de mi equipo sugieren que, entre estos riesgos, se encuentra el trastorno de estrés postraumático, que puede hacer que su cerebro envejezca más rápido

El trastorno de estrés postraumático entre los socorristas El trastorno de estrés postraumático, también conocido como TEPT , es un trastorno de salud mental complejo que puede desarrollarse después de vivir o presenciar un evento traumático
El trauma psicológico se refiere a los efectos emocionales duraderos de la exposición directa o indirecta a circunstancias que ponen en peligro la vida o a la violencia
El TEPT puede manifestarse con recuerdos intrusivos, evitación, estado de alerta elevado, problemas para dormir y cambios en el estado de ánimo y el pensamiento
La ansiedad y la depresión suelen presentarse junto con el TEPT
Alrededor del 23 % de los socorristas del World Trade Center han sido diagnosticados con TEPT
En comparación, se estima que alrededor del 6 % de la población general de EE
UU. ha padecido TEPT a lo largo de su vida
Cuando hablo con los socorristas del 11 de septiembre, describen su TEPT y sus dificultades cognitivas como problemas interrelacionados que siguen afectando sus vidas hasta el día de hoy

Esos recuerdos traumáticos siguen siendo vívidos, y algunos socorristas continúan experimentando ansiedad, depresión, pensamientos intrusivos, problemas para dormir y dificultad para controlar sus emociones
El trauma acelera el envejecimiento cerebral A medida que envejecen, muchos de los socorristas del 11 de septiembre también han notado que su memoria, concentración y agudeza mental se deterioran
Cada vez les preocupa más perder su independencia
En lugar de presentarse como afecciones separadas, las enfermedades físicas, los cambios cognitivos y el malestar emocional a menudo se refuerzan entre sí
En otro estudio, investigadores de mi equipo monitorearon la función cognitiva de más de 5,000 socorristas del World Trade Center sin demencia entre 2014 y 2022
A lo largo de aproximadamente cinco años, 228 desarrollaron demencia antes de los 65 años

Los socorristas con la exposición más grave al polvo y escombros potencialmente neurotóxicos en la zona cero presentaron una incidencia de demencia sustancialmente mayor que aquellos con exposición mínima o que utilizaron de manera constante equipo de protección personal, como respiradores
Esta relación se mantuvo después de controlar los factores demográficos, de estilo de vida, médicos y genéticos
Antes de empezar a estudiar los efectos del 11 de septiembre en la salud, estaba investigando a trabajadores expuestos a metales neurotóxicos y contaminación industrial en el norte de Italia

Al conocer las toxinas dañinas presentes en el polvo del World Trade Center, comencé a preguntarme si los socorristas del 11 de septiembre podrían enfrentar riesgos similares a largo plazo para su cerebro

Esa preocupación se intensificó cuando las tomografías cerebrales de ambos grupos mostraron un aumento similar en los depósitos de una proteína relacionada con la enfermedad de Alzheimer y el deterioro cognitivo llamada beta-amiloide
CEl trabajador de la construcción James Nolan es uno de los socorristas del 11 de septiembre que enfermaron a causa del polvo tóxico y los escombros del World Trade Center

AP Photo/David Goldman Una investigación de mi equipo también reveló que los cerebros de los hombres que participaron en las labores de rescate del 11 de septiembre y que padecían TEPT presentaban resultados de resonancia magnética que indicaban cerebros de mayor edad en comparación con los que no padecían TEPT
En ese estudio de 2025, medimos las estructuras cerebrales mediante resonancias magnéticas y un modelo de inteligencia artificial para estimar la edad cerebral de cada participante

El modelo de inteligencia artificial había sido entrenado para predecir la edad cronológica de una persona a partir de la estructura general de su cerebro, basándose en datos de más de 11 500 resonancias magnéticas cerebrales de personas sanas de entre 5 y 95 años
Utilizamos la diferencia entre la edad cerebral predicha de una persona y su edad real como medida del envejecimiento cerebral acelerado
También observamos que los socorristas con TEPT tenían cerebros que parecían aproximadamente tres años más viejos que su edad cronológica
Por el contrario, la edad cerebral estimada de los socorristas sin TEPT coincidía aproximadamente con su edad cronológica real

<title>The Pentagon is using polygraphs to hunt leakers, but the tests are more theater than fact</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758926/original/file-20260909-50-jyppfa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5770%2C3846&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Polygraphs measure heart rate, blood pressure and perspiration, though there are no specific physiological reactions associated with lying.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/at-daytime-suspicious-man-passes-lie-detector-in-royalty-free-image/1180957596">standret/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In August 2026, government investigators subjected roughly 50 military officers and civilian employees on the Joint Staff to polygraph tests as part of an <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/04/us/politics/pentagon-staff-polygraph-tests.html">inquiry into press leaks</a> about the Iran war and depleted U.S. munitions, according to The New York Times. The newspaper described the scope of the investigation as unprecedented in the modern military.</p>

<p>This is not the first time the Trump administration <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/with-polygraphs-probes-trump-administration-chases-even-minor-leaks-2025-05-23/">has used polygraphs</a> in this way; in 2025, it directed that a wave of tests be administered <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2025-05-23/with-polygraphs-and-probes-trump-administration-chases-even-minor-leaks">across the executive branch</a> to expose minor leaks.</p>

<p>As someone who has taken roughly a dozen polygraphs during my 27-year <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/brian-c-oneill/">career with the CIA</a>, I am wary of how the process is understood – and of the certainty its use can appear to convey.</p>

<p>Polygraphs carry an ominous, almost mythological reputation among Americans. The more familiar and unofficial term – <a href="https://www.apa.org/topics/cognitive-neuroscience/polygraph">lie detector tests</a> – likely fuels that perception. <a href="https://theconversation.com/lie-detection-tests-have-worked-the-same-way-for-3-000-years-and-theyre-still-hopelessly-inaccurate-200741">Television crime dramas</a> have done their part, too, often portraying the device as an oracle for uncovering the truth when conventional methods fail. </p>

<p>In those portrayals, the polygraph is not merely a tool – it’s a window into the soul.</p>

<p>Among those entering government service, especially in national security, the greater anxiety is not the background check but passing the polygraph. My advice is always the same: Don’t lie. It’s the best – and perhaps only – guidance for a process that most assessments have <a href="https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/10420/chapter/1">concluded is a more subjective interpretation than empirical science</a>. </p>

<h2>Why the polygraph persists</h2>

<p>Polygraphs are “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsisyn.2024.100479">pseudo-scientific</a>” in that they measure physiological responses such as heart rate, blood pressure and perspiration. The assumption is that liars betray themselves through spikes in those signals. But this presumes a kind of psychological transparency that simply doesn’t hold up. A person might sweat and tremble simply from fear, anger or frustration – not deceit.</p>

<p>There also are no specific physiological reactions associated with lying. The <a href="https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/10420/chapter/1">National Academy of Sciences</a> in 2003, and the <a href="https://www.apa.org/topics/cognitive-neuroscience/polygraph">American Psychological Association</a> in a 2004 review, concluded that the polygraph rests more on theater than fact. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/lhb0000307">A 2019 assessment</a> reached the same conclusion.</p>

<p>Accordingly, polygraph results are <a href="https://www.lawinfo.com/resources/criminal-defense/are-lie-detector-tests-admissible-in-court.html">not generally admissible in U.S. courts</a>. Only a handful of states – such as Georgia, Arizona and California – permit their use even under limited conditions. And they typically require that both parties agree to admission and a judge to approve it. Unconditional admissibility remains the exception, not the rule.</p>

<p>And yet, inside many national security agencies, polygraphs remain central to the clearance process – a fact I observed firsthand during my time overseeing personnel vetting and analytic hiring within the intelligence community.</p>

<p>While not treated as conclusive, polygraph results often serve as a filter. A candidate’s visible discomfort – or the examiner’s subjective judgment that a response seems evasive – can stall or end the hiring process. For instance, I know that government agencies have halted clearances after an examiner flagged elevated reactions to questions about past drug use or foreign contacts, even when no disqualifying behavior was ultimately documented. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Exterior view of a federal building with an American flag flying on a mast." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678651/original/file-20250707-56-r5gkhb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The FBI’s J. Edgar Hoover headquarters building in Washington in 2016.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/FundedbyISIS/fc97f9ba8657409190a1400b245baccc/photo?Query=FBI%20building&amp;mediaType=photo&amp;sortBy=&amp;dateRange=Anytime&amp;totalCount=900&amp;currentItemNo=10">AP Photo/Cliff Owen</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In some cases, an examiner’s suggestion that a chart shows an anomaly has led otherwise strong applicants to volunteer details they hadn’t planned to share – such as minor security infractions, undeclared relationships, or casual drug use from decades earlier – that, while not disqualifying on their own, reshape how their trustworthiness is perceived.</p>

<p>The polygraph’s power lies in creating the conditions under which deception is confessed.</p>

<h2>A predictable pattern</h2>

<p>No administration has been immune to <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2019/10/08/trump-obsession-polygraphs-leaks-038431">the impulse to investigate leaks</a>. The reflex is bipartisan and familiar: An embarrassing disclosure appears in the press – contradicting official statements or exposing internal dissent – and the White House vows to identify and punish the source. Polygraphs are often part of this ritual.</p>

<p>During his first term, <a href="https://www.politico.com/story/2017/07/25/anthony-scaramucci-changes-white-house-communications-office-240928">Trump intensified efforts</a> to expose internal dissent and media leaks. Department guidelines were revised to make it easier for <a href="https://www.rcfp.org/trump-press-freedom-border/">agencies to obtain journalists’ phone and email records</a>, and polygraphs were reportedly used to pressure officials suspected of talking to the press. That trend has continued – and, since 2025, escalated.</p>

<p>Policies at the Pentagon now <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/pentagon-will-remove-media-offices-after-judge-reinstates-nyts-press-credentials">restrict unescorted press access</a>, revoke office space for major outlets and favor ideologically aligned networks. The line between legitimate leak prevention and the surveillance or sidelining of critical press coverage has grown increasingly blurred.</p>

<p>At agencies such as the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/dhs-kristi-noem-employee-polygraph-tests-7249fc38?mod=Searchresults_pos8&amp;page=1">Department of Homeland Security</a> and the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/apr/29/fbi-polygraph-test-leaks">FBI</a>, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/01/us/politics/fbi-patel.html">polygraphs reportedly have been used frequently</a> – and more punitively – to identify internal dissenters. Even “<a href="https://www.axios.com/2025/05/27/fbi-white-house-cocaine-supreme-court-leak-investigations">cold cases</a>,” such as the leak of the <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2023/01/supreme-court-investigators-fail-to-identify-who-leaked-dobbs-opinion/">Supreme Court’s Dobbs opinion</a> ahead of its overturning of Roe v. Wade, were reopened, despite prior investigations yielding no definitive source.</p>

<h2>Government reaction varies</h2>

<p>Not all leaks are treated the same. Disclosures that align with official narratives or offer strategic advantage may be quietly tolerated, even if unauthorized. Others, especially those that embarrass senior officials or reveal dysfunction, are more likely to prompt formal investigation. </p>

<p>In 2003, for example, the leak of CIA officer Valerie Plame’s identity – widely seen as <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/style/valerie-plame-americas-most-famous-ex-spy-finds-her-new-identity/2019/12/01/2d29086a-0177-11ea-8bab-0fc209e065a8_story.html">retaliation for her husband’s criticism of the Iraq War</a> – triggered a federal investigation. The disclosure embarrassed senior officials, led to <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/scooter-libby-loses-law-license-due-to-perjury/">White House aide Scooter Libby’s conviction for perjury</a>, later commuted, and drew <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2005/07/16/politics/state-dept-memo-gets-scrutiny-in-leak-inquiry-on-cia-officer.html">intense political scrutiny</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man dressed in a suit and tie rides in the back seat of a car." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=533&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=533&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/678647/original/file-20250707-56-sshob7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=533&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Lewis Libby, Vice President Dick Cheney’s chief of staff, rides in the backseat of a limousine on Oct. 27, 2005, in McLean, Va.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="http://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/lewis-libby-vice-president-dick-cheneys-chief-of-staff-news-photo/56020488?adppopup=true">Win McNamee/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Leaks involving classified material draw the sharpest response when they challenge presidential authority or expose internal disputes. That was the case in 2010 with <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2017/06/12/magazine/the-long-lonely-road-of-chelsea-manning.html">Chelsea Manning</a>, whose disclosure of diplomatic cables and battlefield reports embarrassed senior officials and sparked global backlash. Government reaction often depends less on what was disclosed than on who disclosed it – and to what effect.</p>

<p>A narrow set of disclosures, such as those involving espionage or operational compromise, <a href="https://connecticutlawreview.law.uconn.edu/2026/05/31/chilling-ambiguity-can-espionage-act-liability-be-imposed-for-reporting-the-news/">elicit broad consensus</a> as grounds for prosecution. But most leaks fall outside that category. Most investigations fade quietly. The public rarely learns what became of them. Occasionally, there is a vague resignation, but direct accountability is rare.</p>

<h2>What the future holds</h2>

<p>The Pentagon polygraph campaign is not likely to eliminate leaks to the press. But it may have a chilling effect that discourages internal candor while diverting investigative energy away from core security priorities.</p>

<p>Even if such campaigns succeed in reducing unauthorized disclosures, they may come at the cost of institutional resilience. Historically, aggressive internal enforcement has been associated with <a href="https://oig.justice.gov/sites/default/files/2024-11/TMPC-2024.pdf">declining morale and reduced information flow</a> – factors that can hinder adaptation to complex threats.</p>

<p>Some researchers have suggested that artificial intelligence may eventually offer <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2020.103250">reliable tools for detecting deception</a> but caution that the technology is nowhere near operational readiness.</p>

<p>For now, institutions will have to contend with the tools they have – imperfect, imprecise and more performative than predictive.</p>

AP Photo/Cliff Owen In some cases, an examiner’s suggestion that a chart shows an anomaly has led otherwise strong applicants to volunteer details they hadn’t planned to share – such as minor security infractions, undeclared relationships, or casual drug use from decades earlier – that, while not disqualifying on their own, reshape how their trustworthiness is perceived
The polygraph’s power lies in creating the conditions under which deception is confessed
A predictable pattern No administration has been immune to the impulse to investigate leaks

The reflex is bipartisan and familiar: An embarrassing disclosure appears in the press – contradicting official statements or exposing internal dissent – and the White House vows to identify and punish the source
During his first term, Trump intensified efforts to expose internal dissent and media leaks

Department guidelines were revised to make it easier for agencies to obtain journalists’ phone and email records , and polygraphs were reportedly used to pressure officials suspected of talking to the press
That trend has continued – and, since 2025, escalated
Policies at the Pentagon now restrict unescorted press access , revoke office space for major outlets and favor ideologically aligned networks
The line between legitimate leak prevention and the surveillance or sidelining of critical press coverage has grown increasingly blurred
At agencies such as the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI , polygraphs reportedly have been used frequently – and more punitively – to identify internal dissenters
Even “ cold cases ,” such as the leak of the Supreme Court’s Dobbs opinion ahead of its overturning of Roe v
Wade, were reopened, despite prior investigations yielding no definitive source
Government reaction varies Not all leaks are treated the same
Disclosures that align with official narratives or offer strategic advantage may be quietly tolerated, even if unauthorized

<title>How heat on the Tibetan Plateau fuels powerful storms in California, half a world away</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758947/original/file-20260909-60-qxmnah.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C3%2C5349%2C3566&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Heavy rain from an atmospheric river sent the Los Angeles River, normally mostly empty, spilling over its sides in February 2024.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-aerial-view-of-the-los-angeles-river-swollen-by-storm-news-photo/1989155402?adppopup=true">Mario Tama/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The Tibetan Plateau may be on the other side of the world from California, but what happens on this high-altitude landscape in Asia can set off a chain of events that fuels powerful atmospheric rivers with flooding rainfall and heavy snow hitting the U.S. West Coast.</p>

<p>My team of atmospheric scientists <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg3577">discovered this connection, and we explain how it works</a> in a new study in the journal Science Advances.  </p>

<h2>California’s unexpected rainfall</h2>

<p>California and its neighbors saw record-breaking precipitation during the <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/why-did-it-rain-so-much-california-during-last-year%E2%80%99s-la-ni%C3%B1a">winters of 2016–2017</a> and <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/event-tracker/atmospheric-rivers-take-chunk-out-california-drought">2022–2023</a> that caused widespread flooding and infrastructure damage.</p>

<p>The U.S. Pacific Coast often gets <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-an-atmospheric-river-a-hydrologist-explains-the-good-and-bad-of-these-storms-and-how-theyre-changing-222249">atmospheric river storms</a> during its winter rainy season, but the events in those years were especially striking because they occurred during <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">La Niña conditions</a>, which are typically associated with relatively dry winters in California. La Niña is El Niño’s cooler counterpart; they are the two extremes of a climate pattern connected to ocean temperatures known as the <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/what-el-nino-southern-oscillation-enso-nutshell">El Niño-Southern Oscillation</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A band of water curves up from the tropical moisture around the equator to douse the California coast." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758923/original/file-20260909-50-mbt67l.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Satellite data shows the moisture in a powerful atmospheric river drenching Northern California on April 6, 2018.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Powerful_Atmospheric_River_Drenches_Northern_California_(NESDIS_2018-04-06).png">NOAA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The two stormy winters highlighted an important limitation in seasonal forecasting: Ocean-based events such as El Niño and La Niña are important, but they don’t tell the whole story. No global computer models <a href="https://vlab.noaa.gov/documents/12910129/48705482/Extraordinary+Tibetan+Plateau+Early-Winter+Heating+Drove+Record-Breaking+Winter+Precipitation+in+California+and+Adjacent+Regions+in+2017+and+2023.pdf">predicted or simulated 2016-2017 and 2022-2023 winter heavy precipitation in California</a> using sea surface temperature.</p>

<h2>What the Tibetan Plateau has to do with it</h2>

<p>Our study provides evidence that unusually warm land temperatures over the Tibetan Plateau in early winter can help set up atmospheric conditions that <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg3577">favor stronger atmospheric rivers</a> along the U.S. Pacific Coast later in the season, increasing the likelihood of extreme precipitation in California and surrounding regions.</p>

<p>We first analyzed observations and found a statistically significant relationship between early-winter land temperatures over the Tibetan Plateau and late-winter precipitation in California. But a statistical relationship alone cannot establish cause and effect, because both could potentially be influenced by another factor.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two pairs of maps show how winter heat on the Tibetan Plateau corresponds with higher precipitation on the U.S. West Coast." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=658&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=658&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=658&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=827&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=827&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758957/original/file-20260909-50-6a3bxk.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=827&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption"></span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg3577">Yongkang Xue, et al., 2026</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Next, we used climate-model experiments to test whether warming over the Tibetan Plateau could actually contribute to the precipitation extremes more than 7,200 miles (11,600 kilometers) away.</p>

<p>When the global Earth system model was driven primarily by sea-surface temperatures, it failed to reproduce either the strong warming over the Tibetan Plateau or the extreme precipitation observed in California. But using observed Tibetan Plateau land temperatures to improve the model’s initial condition, it reproduced both the observed early-winter warming there and the <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg3577">late-winter precipitation</a> over California. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Livestock on a wide plain with rivers below." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758921/original/file-20260909-60-5jg8tw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Yaks graze on the Tibetan Plateau in Asia.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Yak_grazing_on_the_Tibetan_Plateau.jpg">Tenace10 via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The connection is possible because the <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/tibetan-plateau">Tibetan Plateau</a> is enormous, covering most of southwest China and parts of neighboring countries, and extremely high in elevation, averaging 14,800 feet (4,500 meters) above sea level. When its land surface becomes unusually warm, it heats the atmosphere above it. That changes the temperature differences between the plateau and the surrounding regions. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map shows a large area largely in China at a high elevation." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=375&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=375&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=375&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758942/original/file-20260909-60-ptdsux.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A topographic map shows the elevation of the Tibetan Plateau, rimmed by the Himalayas to the south and west.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tibet_and_surrounding_areas_topographic_map_3.png">darekk2, using NOAA data</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>These changes <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00382-023-06905-5">can disturb the jet stream</a>, the fast-moving westerly current of air in the atmosphere that helps steer weather systems around the Northern Hemisphere. That disturbance can travel eastward from the Tibetan Plateau as a large-scale atmospheric wave, known as a <a href="https://www.ioes.ucla.edu/article/tibetan-plateau-soil-temperatures-are-found-to-affect-climate-regionally-globally/">Tibetan Plateau-Rocky Mountain Wave train</a>.</p>

<p>By the time it reaches the eastern Pacific, the wave can become unstable and “break,” somewhat like an ocean wave breaking nearshore. This changes the structure and stability of the atmosphere over the Pacific and creates conditions that <a href="http://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeg3577">can strengthen atmospheric rivers</a>.</p>

<h2>Better forecasting of atmospheric rivers</h2>

<p>Atmospheric rivers are long, narrow corridors in the sky that transport enormous amounts of water vapor. When they reach the West Coast, they can deliver intense rain and snow.</p>

<p>Many previous studies have shown that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/2014JD022023">atmospheric rivers are central to California’s largest precipitation events</a>. Our findings suggest that early-winter warming over the Tibetan Plateau can help amplify the large-scale atmospheric conditions that make these storms particularly strong.</p>

<p>This connection could also improve forecasting. Forecast systems have traditionally relied heavily on ocean conditions, particularly the El Niño-Southern Oscillation. Our results suggest that land conditions thousands of miles away may provide an additional clue to what’s coming.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A view of the plateau from space" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758938/original/file-20260909-50-keaxah.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Himalayas separate the Tibetan Plateau from the Indian subcontinent in this photo shot from the International Space Station.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/himalayas-separate-tibetan-plateau-from-indian-subcontinent/">NASA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Conditions on the Tibetan Plateau also affect weather in other regions of the world, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-D-21-0270.1">including the East Asian Monsoon</a>. Our past research found a similar pattern of <a href="http://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/11/4/044018">Rocky Mountain spring temperatures influencing</a> weather patterns in the U.S. Southern Plains.</p>

<p>Monitoring Tibetan Plateau temperatures in early winter, together with ocean and atmospheric conditions, could help forecasters better assess the risk of extreme West Coast precipitation later in the season. Incorporating these land signals into forecasting systems could ultimately provide communities, water managers and emergency planners with more time to prepare for damaging atmospheric river seasons.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291438/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Are too many Americans taking antidepressants?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758503/original/file-20260908-50-akahsx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=7%2C0%2C6033%2C4022&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Rates of anxiety and depression have grown since the COVID-19 pandemic – as have prescriptions for antidepressants.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/african-american-woman-hold-glas-of-water-and-royalty-free-image/1539915867">brizmaker/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Drugs for treating depression are among the most prescribed category of medications in the U.S. – <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjment-2025-302287">1 in 6 American adults take them</a>. </p>

<p>Some health researchers and advocates have raised concerns that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2021.0823">too many patients are using antidepressants</a> and that patients who want to stop taking them <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/hex.13966">struggle to do so</a>. One of the most prominent voices on this point is Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who <a href="https://www.medpagetoday.com/psychiatry/depression/121129">launched an effort in May 2026</a> encouraging doctors to <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/07/13/hhs-ssri-deprescribing-experts-gather-clinical-withdrawal-guidance/">find other ways besides antidepressants and other psychiatric drugs</a> to treat depression when possible. </p>

<p>As a  <a href="https://campus.und.edu/directory/andrew.mclean">psychiatrist for over 35 years</a>, including a past role as the medical director of North Dakota’s Department of Human Services, I’ve seen both the benefits and the problems with antidepressants. In my view, there are grains of truth to claims that they are overused, but the full picture is much more nuanced.</p>



<h2>What are antidepressants, and who takes them?</h2>

<p>Over <a href="https://www.truveta.com/blog/research/research-insights/mental-health-prescribing-trends/">half of all antidepressant medications prescribed</a> are a type of drug called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. The first SSRI – fluoxetine, better known by its brand name Prozac – was approved in 1987. A handful of other types of SSRIs, which work through different mechanisms, also exists.</p>

<p>Antidepressants can be <a href="https://theconversation.com/depression-too-often-gets-deemed-hard-to-treat-when-medication-falls-short-198282">helpful for moderate to severe depression</a>, but they are <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK361016/">typically not warranted for mild depression</a>, as the side effects might outweigh any potential benefits. For mild depression, many effective nonmedication treatments exist. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/LF6KCP4WH5w?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has encouraged doctors to steer patients away from antidepressants when possible.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>However, the <a href="https://theconversation.com/when-does-clinical-depression-become-an-emergency-4-questions-answered-200231">distinction between mild and more severe symptoms</a> sometimes gets lost. In everyday language, people use the term “depression” to describe everything from a minor sense of the blahs to a serious clinical condition requiring treatment.</p>

<p>Healthcare workers in primary care clinics routinely screen patients for depression using a widely used questionnaire. This tool can be effective in flagging patients who might need further testing or treatment. But in my experience, if used on its own to diagnose, it can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2020.02.002">be easily misinterpreted</a>.</p>

<p>A person having a bad week or two who scores higher on a screening test might be prescribed a medication that was not necessary. But the tool can also fail to flag people who do need care. Over <a href="https://theconversation.com/suicide-has-reached-epidemic-proportions-in-the-us-yet-medical-students-still-dont-receive-adequate-training-to-treat-suicidal-patients-216603">a third of people who die by suicide</a> have <a href="https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.86356">visited a primary care provider in the month</a> before their death. For those 55 and older, it <a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.159.6.909">rises to more than two-thirds</a>.</p>

<h2>Prescribing in general practice</h2>

<p>According to a 2026 analysis, most prescriptions for antidepressants in the U.S. <a href="https://healthcostinstitute.org/all-hcci-reports/primary-care-providers-prescribe-the-majority-of-antidepressants-and-anxiolytics-for-people-with-employer-sponsored-insurance/">are not written by psychiatrists</a>. In some cases, these medicines are prescribed by nurse practitioners or physician assistants with psychiatric qualifications, but most are written by primary care providers, who are not specialists in mental health. </p>

<p>Clinicians who provide primary care don’t just have less time to evaluate patients’ mental health concerns. They also have less access to ways of treating depression apart from medication, such as talk therapy. </p>

<p>Primary clinics that <a href="https://aims.uw.edu/evidence-base-for-cocm">have behavioral health providers and consult with psychiatrists</a> tend to help patients more effectively and provide more treatment options. These types of collaborative approaches to care are still rare but are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000032554">becoming more common</a>. </p>

<p>I recall my father, who was a country doctor in general practice, saying that half of his patients’ problems had to do with mental health issues, and he didn’t know how best to help them. Today’s primary care providers do receive more training on mental health issues, and they are often more equipped to recommend lifestyle changes that can be especially helpful for people with less severe depression symptoms. </p>

<p>But it’s simply human nature that when given a choice between taking a daily medication and engaging in activities that require commitment and intention, many will choose medication.</p>

<h2>The opposing forces of stigma and access</h2>

<p>Stigma has been a <a href="https://theconversation.com/psychologists-are-starting-to-talk-publicly-about-their-own-mental-illnesses-and-patients-can-benefit-177716">long-standing barrier</a> in seeking mental healthcare. </p>

<p>Since the COVID-19 pandemic, anxiety and depression have become more prevalent. That’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2023-064245">particularly true among adolescents and young adults</a> – especially young women, who <a href="https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2023-064245">tend to experience less stigma</a> around mental health issues. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.kff.org/medicare/what-to-know-about-medicare-coverage-of-telehealth/">New rules during the pandemic</a> also made it <a href="https://theconversation.com/online-therapy-having-its-moment-bringing-insights-on-how-to-expand-mental-health-services-going-forward-136374">significantly easier for people to access</a> mental health treatment – both therapy and medications – remotely, via telehealth. Such access continues to grow. Before the pandemic, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000042305">only 1% to 2% of antidepressant medications</a> were prescribed via telehealth. By 2022, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.33334">it was roughly one-third</a>.</p>

<p>Given these trends, and the fact that clinicians often turn to medication for treating depression regardless of the severity, the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(24)00245-1">uptick in antidepressant prescriptions since 2020</a> should come as no surprise. Virtual visits allow people to navigate more easily around stigma and find increased and convenient access to care. And <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S1463423618000403">many people feel more comfortable</a> getting such care in a primary care clinic rather than a mental health clinic.</p>

<h2>Systemic issues drive prescribing</h2>

<p>For all these reasons, I would say that antidepressant medications are likely overused in some cases. Undoubtedly, some people who take them either don’t benefit from them or could address their symptoms in other ways. </p>

<p>On the other hand, expanded access to mental healthcare – including medication – has also enabled people who need treatment to receive it. Even now, many Americans with serious depression <a href="https://www.samhsa.gov/blog/release-2024-nsduh-leveraging-latest-substance-use-mental-health-data-make-america-healthy-again">receive no or limited treatment</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Older man sitting in an armchair across from a therapist, talking and holding a tissue" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758515/original/file-20260908-50-wd2bpt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">For people with mild depression, medication may not be the best option, but the distinction between mild and more severe symptoms sometimes gets lost.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/mature-man-crying-during-therapy-session-with-royalty-free-image/2207702996">Dimensions/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What’s more, in my view, this imbalance reflects systemic problems in the U.S. healthcare system at least as much as physicians’ prescribing habits or patients’ requests. </p>

<p>For example, primary care clinics are a great place to screen for mental health issues, but getting proper treatment may involve more specialized care – which many patients can’t access. And on the business side, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-024-02321-8">clinicians get little support</a> in helping patients with lifestyle changes and nonmedication treatments – rather than prescribing drugs. </p>

<h2>Difficulties in ditching antidepressants</h2>

<p>Kennedy has claimed that for some people, stopping antidepressants can be <a href="https://theconversation.com/robert-f-kennedy-jr-says-antidepressants-are-harder-to-quit-than-heroin-is-he-right-248937">harder than quitting heroin</a>. Research suggests such extreme effects of discontinuing medication are rare, though not unheard of. </p>

<p>Any time a person is on a medication for a significant period of time, the brain and body <a href="https://www.verywellhealth.com/drug-tolerance-5271896">adapt to establish a new balance</a>. This happens with other substances, too – as any regular coffee drinker who has tried abruptly quitting knows.</p>

<p>People who want to stop taking antidepressants after being on them for a long time generally do best when they gradually taper their dose over weeks to months, unless they have a specific reason for stopping more quickly. </p>

<p>For antidepressants, clinicians watch for <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/25218-antidepressant-discontinuation-syndrome">withdrawal symptoms</a> including sleep problems, flu-like symptoms, headaches and an electrical buzzing sensation in the head. A 2024 review of dozens of rigorous studies that compared the experiences of people taking antidepressants with those taking a sugar pill found that roughly a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(24)00133-0">quarter of people stopping antidepressants</a> experienced some withdrawal symptoms, and for 3%, they were severe. </p>

<p>While certain antidepressants might be more likely to cause withdrawal symptoms, it’s tough to tell who might have the most difficulty. And for some patients, depression is a chronic illness for which they must take medication indefinitely.</p>

<p>However, most people working with an experienced clinician are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(24)00133-0">able to successfully discontinue these drugs</a>. Ultimately, what’s most important is that patients are able to consult with a knowledgeable provider in making that decision.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/284992/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Andrew McLean has taken part in projects that have included government funded grants related to mental health and substance misuse and holds an Endowed Chair in Neuroscience funded in part by the Neuropsychiatric Research Institute through the UND Alumni Association and Foundation.</span></em></p></content>

title: 2026’s El Niño is shaping up to be a doozy – it’s already affecting global shipping, fish behavior and heat

<title>2026’s El Niño is shaping up to be a doozy – it’s already affecting global shipping, fish behavior and heat</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758972/original/file-20260909-50-gvrpvi.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3064%2C2042&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">With deepening drought, worsened by El Niño, Panama Canal authorities cut the number of ships allowed to transit.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/aerial-view-of-the-one-contribution-container-ship-sailing-news-photo/2271855697?adppopup=true">Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>El Niño is here, and forecasters warn that it’s likely to be bigger and stronger in 2026-27 than any El Niño event recorded in at least 150 years. </p>

<p>During <a href="https://www.noaa.gov/understanding-el-nino">strong El Niños</a>, global air and ocean temperatures spike, and precipitation patterns shift dramatically – flooding rains deluge places that are normally dry, and drought strikes some of the wettest locations on earth. With this El Niño arriving on top of <a href="https://climatereanalyzer.org/clim/sst_daily/?dm_id=world2">already high global ocean</a> and <a href="https://climatereanalyzer.org/clim/t2_daily/?dm_id=world">air temperatures</a>, it carries the potential for extraordinary impacts to millions of lives throughout the world. Globally, August 2026 was the <a href="https://climate.copernicus.eu/copernicus-august-was-worlds-joint-hottest-month-record-pushing-global-temperatures-back-above">hottest month on record</a>, according to data from Europe’s Copernicus climate service.</p>

<p>Those effects are already showing up in Central and South America. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Fishermen in small boats in a harbor." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758973/original/file-20260909-50-wystcb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Ecuadorian fishing boats have found that they have to go farther from shore to make their catch as the fish move to cooler zones.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fisherman-sits-in-a-boat-at-the-santa-rosa-fishing-port-in-news-photo/2161028069?adppopup=true">Enrique Ortiz/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Fishing crews in Ecuador are <a href="http://ecuavisa.com/ecuador/pesca-ecuatoriana-enfrenta-menor-captura-de-atun-por-el-calentamiento-del-mar-y-el-nino-20260824-0093.html">catching fewer tuna and traveling farther</a> from shore to find them as fish migrate to cooler water. Coral reefs are under alert for <a href="https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_baa-max-7d.php">severe risk of bleaching</a> in many areas.</p>

<p>In Panama, where I live, seabirds common to Ecuador and Peru known as blue-footed boobies began <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/environment/displaced-by-el-nio-south-american-seabirds-flock-panama-2026-08-14/">showing up in large numbers in Panama</a> earlier than usual as the sardines and anchovies they eat moved northward to escape the El Niño ocean heat. </p>

<p>Farmers in some regions of Panama have been <a href="https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20260826-panama-and-el-salvador-declare-emergency-over-el-nino-fuelled-drought">unable to plant their crops</a>. And many people here are worried about access to drinking water in the coming dry season, normally January to April but predicted to arrive at least a month earlier than usual.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A bird with blue feet stands on a rock." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=426&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=426&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=426&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=536&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=536&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758320/original/file-20260908-50-rg5w1i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=536&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
