              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Blue-footed_booby_01.jpg">Bernard Gagnon via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The global economy is also beginning to see far-reaching effects. Worsening drought is reducing the amount of water needed to operate the Panama Canal, resulting in <a href="https://pancanal.com/en/panama-canal-adopts-additional-measures-to-address-reduced-precipitation-in-the-canal-watershed/">fewer ships with less cargo able to pass through in a day</a>. That leads to higher transit costs for shippers of all kinds of products and slower deliveries.</p>

<p>I am <a href="https://profiles.si.edu/display/nPatonS872006">a biologist</a> who has been monitoring the weather in Panama and surrounding regions for the <a href="https://stri.si.edu/">Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute</a> for almost 40 years. That includes major climatic events such as El Niño, and what I am seeing in Panama in 2026 in terms of heat and drought has already begun to exceed anything that we have measured here in over a century.</p>

<h2>What is El Niño?</h2>

<p>El Niño is a <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/ninonina.html">naturally occurring phenomenon</a> that can <a href="https://www.weather.gov/fwd/teleconnections">affect weather around the world</a>. Its origin lies in the tropical belt of the Pacific Ocean.</p>

<p>Normally, trade winds along the equator blow from east to west in this region, pushing warm surface water toward the islands of southeast Asia, where it accumulates. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/WPA-KpldDVc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">What is El Niño?</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The first sign that El Niño is developing is <a href="https://youtu.be/WPA-KpldDVc?si=mY8S6OjIKHfVY-3_">a weakening, or even reversal, of the tropical Pacific trade winds</a>. Without the winds, warm water in the east begins to flow back and eventually occupies much of the equatorial waters down to about 300 meters from the coast of South America to the middle of the Pacific.</p>

<p>That shift sets off a chain of changes in weather patterns around the world.</p>

<h2>What can El Niño do to – or for – you?</h2>

<p>According to predictions from the <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml">National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration</a> (NOAA), as well as many <a href="https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/blog/2026/an-unprecedented-el-nio-and-its-implications-for-the-weather-forecast">other national</a> and <a href="https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/strong-el-nino-expected-intensify">international climate authorities</a>, the earth and its inhabitants can expect one of the warmest, if not the hottest, years on record both in 2026 and 2027.</p>

<p>Global ocean temperatures are <a href="https://climatereanalyzer.org/clim/sst_daily/?dm_id=world2">already at record highs</a>, raising concerns about the compounding effects of El Niño and global warming effects on <a href="https://theconversation.com/el-nino-is-back-and-ocean-temperatures-are-already-near-record-highs-that-can-spell-disaster-for-fish-and-corals-285097">corals and other sea life</a>, particularly along the west coast of the Americas and Australia.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Chart of all years since 1981 show the last four were exceptionally warm for the oceans" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=363&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=363&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=363&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=456&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=456&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/758337/original/file-20260908-50-kgd6n6.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=456&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some of the wettest regions on the planet, including southeast Asia, Australia, northern South America, Central America and the Caribbean, are expected to experience <a href="https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027">severe droughts this year</a>.</p>

<p>Places that are normally extremely dry, such as the coasts of Ecuador and Peru, may face strong storms with the potential for life-threatening floods.</p>

<h2>Why it’s hard to forecast El Niño and its effects</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/what-el-nino-southern-oscillation-enso-nutshell">El Niño-Southern Oscillation</a> – the climate system that swings between warm El Niño and cooler La Niña conditions every few years – like many things in nature, is extremely complex. Scientists have been studying it for generations, and many things about it are still not fully understood.</p>

<p>Forecasters, such as NOAA, use many different computer models to help predict how complex systems like this will unfold. Each model differs in the details of how they make their predictions, and the average of the models forms the basis of the predictions presented to the public.</p>

<p><iframe id="sk1it" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sk1it/4/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="NOAA's September El Nino forecast"></iframe></p>

<p>It is important to understand that these are best estimates based on the available knowledge and understanding.</p>

<p>Every El Niño is different. They can vary significantly between one event and another both in timing and impact. Each El Niño seems to include some unexpected results, especially regarding where droughts and floods appear. Some effects, such as drought in Central America and global air temperature spikes, are almost guaranteed. Others, such as heavy rainfall on the U.S. West Coast, are more variable. For example, the <a href="https://www.conservation.ca.gov/cgs/landslides/el-nino">2015-16 El Niño</a>, one of the strongest on record, brought little relief to drought-stricken California.</p>

<p>So, do not assume that what usually happens at your location during El Niño will happen this time.</p>

<h2>The super, mega El Niño of 2026-27</h2>

<p>To gauge the intensity of an El Niño event, scientists look at the temperatures in the middle of the equatorial Pacific in a region known as <a href="https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/4695">Niño 3.4</a>. </p>

<p>The intensity of an El Niño event is defined as the current or expected sea surface temperatures in that region minus the long-term average. A very strong event is considered to have a value of at least 2 Celsius – meaning it’s 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the average.</p>

<p><iframe id="YcCy4" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/YcCy4/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="El Nino and La Nina over time"></iframe></p>

<p>In the past century, two El Niño events stand out – <a href="https://www.whoi.edu/science/b/people/kamaral/1982-1983ElNino.html">1982-83</a> and <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/2015-state-climate-el-ni%C3%B1o-came-saw-and-conquered">2015-16</a> – each with values close to 2.6 C (4.7 F).</p>

<p>Predictions for the current event include from around 3 C to almost 4 C (5.4 – 7.2 F), potentially placing it well above anything that has occurred in at least 150 years, and <a href="https://theconversation.com/galapagos-corals-show-el-nino-events-are-more-extreme-now-than-in-past-1-000-years-heres-how-my-team-made-the-discovery-272318">likely much longer</a>.</p>

<h2>This matters to the global economy</h2>

<p>The influences of El Niño should raise global alarms for economies as well.</p>

<p>The Panama Canal is one of the world’s most important shipping choke points, particularly for ships traveling to and from the U.S. It relies exclusively on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its <a href="https://pancanal.com/en/design-of-the-locks/">system of locks</a>, which act like elevators – filling with water to lift each ship 85 feet (26 meters) from sea level to the lake and then back down to sea level on the other side. The canal saves <a href="https://www.allisonshipping.com/insights/the-strategic-gateway-why-the-panama-canal-still-matters-in-international-shipping/">days of travel time and hundreds of thousands of dollars in fuel costs</a> as ships travel between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.</p>

<p>Panama is normally so rainy that the locks can function at full capacity throughout the year. During droughts, however, the lake levels can begin to fall even during the rainy season when they should be going up. </p>

<p>Once lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority, the agency in charge of the canal, begins to restrict their maximum draft, meaning how deep into the water the ships sink when loaded. Even before then, it starts to <a href="https://apps.pancanal.com/t/TI/views/GatunH2OIndicators/GatunWaterLevel?%3AisGuestRedirectFromVizportal=y&amp;%3Aembed=y">reduce the number of ships</a> that can pass each day in order to save water. </p>

<p><iframe id="GoizP" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GoizP/4/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Lake Gatun's water levels during El Nino years. Low levels mean less ship traffic"></iframe></p>

<p>Previous major El Niños have resulted in <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/panama-canal-el-nino/a-78453054">significant interruptions to the canal’s operations</a>. This year is no exception. The Panama Canal Authority has already <a href="https://pancanal.com/en/panama-canal-adopts-additional-measures-to-address-reduced-precipitation-in-the-canal-watershed/">begun to restrict the number and size of ships</a> allowed to pass in 2026. As El Niño intensifies, these limits will only become tighter.</p>

<p>As what could be the strongest El Niño on record develops, families, communities and economies need to prepare. Local areas may see more intense effects than expected, or they may see different effects than in past El Niños. The best preparation is to be ready for the worst and pay attention to the forecasts.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291490/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Pennsylvania’s aging levees are under pressure from scarce funding and severe weather</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757589/original/file-20260902-60-bjqmrw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The Schuylkill River in Philadelphia flooded after heavy rains from Hurricane Ida in 2021.

</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/water-from-the-schuylkill-river-covers-the-schuylkill-river-news-photo/1235030768">Branden Eastwood/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Pennsylvania has over <a href="https://levees.sec.usace.army.mil">180 levees</a> that span approximately 155 miles (255 kilometers) and keep its rivers from flooding. They <a href="https://levees.sec.usace.army.mil">protect about 158,000 people and US$26.2 billion in property</a> across the state, according to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. </p>

<p>However, those levees are aging, and funding to maintain and improve them is becoming scarcer.</p>

<p>At the same time, extreme weather is becoming <a href="https://theconversation.com/severe-storms-battered-pittsburgh-twice-as-often-as-usual-this-spring-a-meteorologist-explains-why-286303">increasingly frequent and severe</a>.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=Lf-Fd94AAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;authuser=1&amp;sortby=pubdate">geotechnical engineer</a> and <a href="https://kaleighyost.com/">geohazards researcher</a>, I study how levees respond to flooding. I also help develop solutions to evaluate, manage and improve aging levee infrastructure.</p>

<p>These solutions are more important than ever as Pennsylvania continues to see <a href="https://www.centredaily.com/news/weather-news/article317115331.html">record rainfall</a> this season.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A small river or stream winds through a wooded and grassy area" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757856/original/file-20260903-50-znl972.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Kaleigh Yost</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/">CC BY-NC-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How levees work</h2>

<p>Levees are earthen embankments positioned parallel to a river that effectively raise the height of the banks of the river to prevent overflow when the river swells.</p>

<p>Typically, levees are designed to prevent flooding from a particular-size flood. Often, that’s a flood that has a 1% chance of occurring in any given year. </p>

<p>Levees can be breached when water flows over the top during flooding. They can also fail due to erosion, water seeping through or under the embankment, and partial collapse of the embankment before floodwater reaches the top. </p>

<p>In Pennsylvania, flooding is a frequent and <a href="https://pafloodrisk.psu.edu/home/">damaging natural hazard</a>. </p>

<p>The state’s <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/programs-and-services/water/bureau-of-waterways-engineering-and-wetlands/stream-and-wetland-regulatory-program/advice-on-flood-prevention-and-management-on-streams/advice-on-flood-prevention-and-management-on-streams">86,000 miles</a> (138,000 kilometers) of rivers and streams commonly surge under heavy rains and snowmelt. Major population centers <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/philadelphia-pennsylvania-news">Philadelphia</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/pittsburgh-news">Pittsburgh</a> both are flanked by rivers. And although Pennsylvania is not thought of as a coastal state, it can be significantly impacted by remnants of hurricanes and tropical storms.</p>

<p>Pennsylvania’s 2023 State Hazard Mitigation Plan has recorded almost <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/pema/ready-communities/mitigation">5,000 flood events</a> in the state since 1996. The National Flood Insurance Program has paid over <a href="https://www.floodsmart.gov/historical-nfip-claims-information-and-trends?map=countries/us/us-pa-all&amp;region=us-pa&amp;miny=1996&amp;maxy=2025&amp;county=&amp;gtype=state">$1 billion in claims</a> to property owners in Pennsylvania over that same time period.</p>

<h2>Aging infrastructure and growing costs</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://www.publications.usace.army.mil/Portals/76/Publications/EngineerPamphlets/EP_870-1-29.pdf">Flood Control Act of 1936</a>, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt as part of his New Deal agenda, was partially motivated by <a href="https://www.usace.army.mil/Media/Fact-Sheets/Fact-Sheets-View/Article/4466597/183-25013-three-key-flood-control-acts-of-the-early-20th-century/">devastating flooding in Pennsylvania</a> that year. The legislation allocated funding for the construction of many of Pennsylvania’s levees. As a result, most levees in Pennsylvania were constructed by the state and federal government <a href="https://infrastructurereportcard.org/state-item/pennsylvania/">between 1950 and 1970</a>. </p>

<p>This means the majority of Pennsylvania’s levees were designed and constructed based on engineering standards and practices from six to eight decades ago, and they have exceeded their typical <a href="https://infrastructurereportcard.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/PA-Report-Card-2022.pdf">design life of 50 years</a>.</p>

<p>After construction of the levees, the federal government transferred responsibility for management and upkeep to local community sponsors. <a href="https://infrastructurereportcard.org/state-item/pennsylvania/">Over 90% of Pennsylvania’s levees</a> are locally operated and maintained. For many rural Pennsylvania communities with <a href="https://www.rural.pa.gov/download.cfm?file=Resources/fact-sheets/Rural%20Aging%20Population%20July%202023.pdf">aging populations</a>, declining tax bases and labor shortages, these costs can be a challenge.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.spa.usace.army.mil/Portals/16/docs/emergencymgmt/LeveeSponsor_Maintenance_Guide.pdf">Maintaining levee embankments</a> isn’t cheap. It requires managing vegetation, controlling erosion, removing debris and repairing animal burrows. Other features of levees, like floodwalls, pump stations and pipes, also require periodic maintenance and upgrades.  </p>

<p>In other words, construction of a levee is not a one-time investment. It is an ongoing commitment that can be expensive as older levees require more repairs and upgrades, and inflation drives up costs.</p>

<h2>Levees not built for today’s flood risks</h2>

<p>Flood risk is understood as a combination of hazard, exposure and vulnerability. All three change over time. </p>

<p>Evolving weather patterns are resulting in more severe flood hazards. As areas protected by levees become more developed, more people and infrastructure are exposed to the hazard. Aging infrastructure increases their vulnerability.</p>

<p>Heavy rainfall across Pennsylvania is increasing. From 1958 to 2021, the amount of rainfall during the top 1% heaviest storms in the Northeast U.S. <a href="https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-matters/extreme-precipitation-in-a-warming-climate?utm_medium=email&amp;utm_campaign=CM+Extreme+Precipitation+in+a+Warming+Climate+2024+EN&amp;utm_content=CM+Extreme+Precipitation+in+a+Warming+Climate+2024+EN+CID_0acb8c6287">increased by 60%</a>, according to the <a href="https://toolkit.climate.gov/sites/default/files/2025-07/NCA5_2023_FullReport.pdf">Fifth National Climate Assessment</a>, published by the U.S. Global Change Research Program. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.fema.gov/">Federal Emergency Management Agency</a> continually updates U.S. floodplain maps to better reflect current risk. These updates can trigger a review of a levee system’s performance. If a community cannot show that its levee meets the minimum design, operations and maintenance requirements outlined in the <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-44/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-65?toc=1">Code of Federal Regulations</a>, areas behind the levee will be considered unprotected against the 1% annual chance flood. This will result in higher <a href="https://www.doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ae2495">flood insurance premiums</a> and development restrictions for homeowners and businesses located behind the “unaccredited” levee. </p>

<p>Currently, only <a href="https://levees.sec.usace.army.mil">around 15%</a> of Pennsylvania’s levees are <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dep/programs-and-services/water/bureau-of-waterways-engineering-and-wetlands/flood-protection/levee-safety">accredited</a> by FEMA. </p>

<p>As FEMA proceeds with floodplain mapping updates in Pennsylvania, the need to pursue accreditation is becoming more pressing for many communities. But the accreditation process can be time-consuming and expensive. Levee sponsors are responsible for hiring a professional engineer to conduct the analyses needed to certify that the levee meets the minimum requirements. If the engineer identifies upgrades needed to meet minimum protection levels, like raising the levee height, the levee sponsors must find funding to make those upgrades.</p>

<h2>Scattered funding for levee repairs and upgrades</h2>

<p>Financial support for levees is <a href="https://infrastructurereportcard.org/cat-item/levees-infrastructure/">lacking nationally</a>. Although Congress <a href="https://www.asce.org/publications-and-news/civil-engineering-source/civil-engineering-magazine/article/2023/01/wrda-2022-act-revises-levee-safety-inland-waterway-programs">reauthorized</a> the <a href="https://www.usace.army.mil/Missions/Civil-Works/Levee-Safety-Program/">National Levee Safety Program</a> until 2028, appropriations have not been made to fully fund it. </p>

<p>No single stream of funding supports levee maintenance and upgrades. Small communities often have to piece together funding from multiple sources in order to complete a needed project.</p>

<p>Communities draw from local taxes or other fees to support their modest flood control budgets and supplement grant funding. Taxes or fees specifically to support levee operations, maintenance or upgrades are uncommon, though one notable exception is the <a href="https://lcfpa.org/levee-fee/">levee fee</a> collected by the Luzerne County Flood Protection Authority in northeastern Pennsylvania. This fee generates revenue used for maintenance and operations of the 16-mile-long (28-kilometer) <a href="https://levees.sec.usace.army.mil/">levee system</a> along the Susquehanna River that protects around 18,000 buildings and over 62,000 people. </p>

<p>Despite the fee, the Luzerne County Flood Protection Authority still has to <a href="https://www.citizensvoice.com/2026/02/18/flood-authority-gets-extension-for-projects-spending-covid-19-funds-from-luzerne-county/">seek grant funding</a> to support large projects.</p>

<p>Some state funding for levee repairs and upgrades is available through the <a href="https://www.houseappropriations.com/Topic/Other/153">Pennsylvania capital budget</a>, but these funds are limited and subject to bureaucratic delays. Some communities obtain grants up to $500,000 from the state’s Department of Community &amp; Economic Development <a href="https://dced.pa.gov/programs/flood-mitigation-program-fmp/">Flood Mitigation Program</a>. The program requires the participating community to match 15% of the total project costs. </p>

<p>The Pennsylvania <a href="https://dced.pa.gov/programs/local-share-account-lsa-statewide/">Local Share Account</a> can also support some levee projects of limited scope.</p>

<p>Starting in 2020, FEMA’s <a href="https://www.fema.gov/grants/mitigation/learn/building-resilient-infrastructure-communities">Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities</a>, or BRIC, program provided an avenue for federal funding for hazard mitigation projects, including levee upgrades. But FEMA announced the elimination of the BRIC program in April 2025 and canceled around <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/05/01/nx-s1-5359452/trump-disaster-funding-cuts-fema-bric">$182.5 million</a> in grants already awarded to Pennsylvania. At least two of those grants were supporting Pennsylvania levee projects: the rehabilitation of the <a href="https://fox56.com/news/local/duryea-awaits-bric-funding-as-fema-returns-amid-dhs-shutdown">Duryea levee</a> in Luzerne County, and construction plans for a <a href="https://www.wnep.com/article/news/local/luzerne-county/fema-funding-cut-leaves-luzerne-county-homes-more-vulnerable-to-flooding-bric-protection-program/523-279b1573-7188-48a0-af8e-dedc7202748b">new levee in nearby Exeter</a>.</p>

<p>Pennsylvania was one of over 20 states that <a href="https://www.floods.org/news-views/fema-news/fema-ordered-to-restart-bric-program/">sued the federal government</a> in response to the termination of the BRIC funding. The <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IN12609">program was reinstated</a> in March 2026 after a judge <a href="https://www.floods.org/news-views/fema-news/fema-ordered-to-restart-bric-program/">ruled the termination unlawful</a>. However, it is unclear how and when funds will be distributed, and whether those funds will <a href="https://www.naco.org/news/counties-regroup-after-femas-resiliency-grant-program-resumes">cover planned project costs</a>.</p>

<h2>Future outlook</h2>

<p>The bottom line is that levees built in the mid-1900s will not continue to provide the same level of flood protection forever. </p>

<p>Communities across Pennsylvania will need innovative solutions to promote flood resilience despite limited financial capacity as their levees continue to age, severe weather worsens and funding remains uncertain. </p>

<p>My colleagues at Penn State and I are working to develop and <a href="https://doi.org/10.17603/ds2-dh71-0s11">deploy new technologies to investigate levee conditions</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s44304-024-00002-1">improve engineering analyses</a> and establish <a href="https://www.psu.edu/our-impact/flooding-prevention-levees">community-centered approaches</a> to address this challenging issue.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi-org.ezaccess.libraries.psu.edu/10.1016/j.enggeo.2019.105206">Geophysical technologies</a> allow you to “see” inside a levee without disturbing the embankment and can be less expensive than traditional methods of levee investigation. These methods use seismic, electrical or magnetic waves to characterize soil layers and their properties. Drones can support collection of highly detailed imagery, topography and even information about <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2024.104982">internal erosion</a>. Advances in these technologies will enable more rapid and robust assessments of levee conditions.</p>

<p>Local leaders understand their community’s unique challenges when it comes to flood resilience – but they need technical support and financial resources to implement solutions. </p>

At the same time, extreme weather is becoming increasingly frequent and severe

Kaleigh Yost , CC BY-NC-SA How levees work Levees are earthen embankments positioned parallel to a river that effectively raise the height of the banks of the river to prevent overflow when the river swells
Typically, levees are designed to prevent flooding from a particular-size flood
Often, that’s a flood that has a 1% chance of occurring in any given year
Levees can be breached when water flows over the top during flooding
They can also fail due to erosion, water seeping through or under the embankment, and partial collapse of the embankment before floodwater reaches the top
In Pennsylvania, flooding is a frequent and damaging natural hazard
The state’s 86,000 miles (138,000 kilometers) of rivers and streams commonly surge under heavy rains and snowmelt
Major population centers Philadelphia and Pittsburgh both are flanked by rivers
And although Pennsylvania is not thought of as a coastal state, it can be significantly impacted by remnants of hurricanes and tropical storms
Pennsylvania’s 2023 State Hazard Mitigation Plan has recorded almost 5,000 flood events in the state since 1996
The National Flood Insurance Program has paid over $1 billion in claims to property owners in Pennsylvania over that same time period
Aging infrastructure and growing costs The Flood Control Act of 1936 , signed by President Franklin D
Roosevelt as part of his New Deal agenda, was partially motivated by devastating flooding in Pennsylvania that year
The legislation allocated funding for the construction of many of Pennsylvania’s levees
As a result, most levees in Pennsylvania were constructed by the state and federal government between 1950 and 1970

This means the majority of Pennsylvania’s levees were designed and constructed based on engineering standards and practices from six to eight decades ago, and they have exceeded their typical design life of 50 years
After construction of the levees, the federal government transferred responsibility for management and upkeep to local community sponsors
Over 90% of Pennsylvania’s levees are locally operated and maintained
For many rural Pennsylvania communities with aging populations , declining tax bases and labor shortages, these costs can be a challenge
Maintaining levee embankments isn’t cheap
It requires managing vegetation, controlling erosion, removing debris and repairing animal burrows
Other features of levees, like floodwalls, pump stations and pipes, also require periodic maintenance and upgrades
In other words, construction of a levee is not a one-time investment
It is an ongoing commitment that can be expensive as older levees require more repairs and upgrades, and inflation drives up costs

title: The one problem Trump can’t afford
excerpt: President Donald Trump points to the crowd after speaking at the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story a
body: President Donald Trump points to the crowd after speaking at the 2026 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Republicans promised their midterm convention would feature lots of President Donald Trump
Night one of “Trumpapalooza” delivered — and then some
For almost two hours Wednesday night, Trump exhorted his base to turn out for November’s down-ballot elections
The meandering, made-for-TV speech hit all his Trumpiest subjects, from immigration and crime to transgender athletes, the White House ballroom, and taxes
But equally notable were the issues he brushed past
The purpose of this convention, after all, was to energize Republican voters whose enthusiasm has flagged
The GOP could lose the House and/or Senate in November, despite its aggressive (and increasingly undemocratic ) efforts to retain them

But Trump skirted several of the topics that voters care about most, like the cost of housing, food, and consumer goods. (More on the politics of affordability below.)  He never said the words “inflation,” “rent,” or “housing,” for instance
He mentioned grocery costs once in passing, when he falsely claimed they were “rapidly” going down
And his 90-second discussion of “affordability” blamed green-energy policies and Democrats for rising prices: “It’s fake
They are so fake,” he said.  Still, Trump does seem to recognize voters’ economic angst
He promised, fantastically and impossibly , to cut everyone $5,000 checks if Republicans hold Congress on Election Day.  Trumpapalooza continues tonight with a keynote by Vice President JD Vance
Personally, I’ll be watching to see if he addresses affordability — or any other important, less-Trumpy topics
Go a little deeper View Link During his first presidential campaign, Trump famously said that he could “stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody” without losing supporters

Now, as his party fights to retain control of Congress, he’s again testing what he can get away with — this time, by repeatedly dismissing Americans’ growing concerns about the cost of food, housing and gasoline
In May, Trump said he wasn’t thinking about Americans’ finances as he negotiated with Iran

Weeks later, as consumer prices rose at their fastest rate in years, he told reporters, “ I love the inflation .”  More recently, Trump and his allies have called affordability a “made-up” word and insisted prices are falling , though most consumer goods cost more now than at the start of his second term

Trump’s rhetoric suggests he “ doesn’t really care about the fate of his party ,” the historian Julian Zelizer told Vox’s Astead Herndon last month — pointing to the high cost of gas, in particular, which has proved the undoing of several prior presidents.   Instead, White House officials and other people close to Trump say that his approach to affordability reflects a more personal concern: how history will remember him and his administration .  “When the president goes down in the history books, it’s not going to be for eggs being a dollar a carton,” Shelby Talcott, Semafor’s White House correspondent, told Vox in June
She was paraphrasing months of her conversations with White House officials, who said Trump prioritized legacy-defining achievements, like denying Iran a nuclear weapon or rehabilitating Venezuela

But there’s an obvious and self-defeating tension here: If the Iran war raises household prices enough to cost Republicans control of Congress, then Trump may lose the opportunity to advance the rest of his agenda
Even Trump may find there are some limits to what he can do without the risk of political consequences
Playfully! For fun! There’s been a boom in so-called social deduction games — like Mafia, Werewolf, and Blood on the Clocktower — which involve deceiving other players
Consider it a lighthearted way to work through the angst of a frequently distrustful and antisocial era

Before you go… Did you know… that for every pig they send to slaughter, US hog farmers must pay roughly $1 to a semi-governmental marketing group called the National Pork Board? It’s an arrangement called a “checkoff” and it’s common in American agriculture

But the Pork Board may have used the program to funnel money to a lobbying group.  Today’s trivia: How old — approximately! — are the world’s oldest known ovens? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the founder of Carthage in Greek mythology
That would be Dido, who — per legend — bargained with a local king for as much land as could fit in an oxhide
She then cut the oxhide into strips and got a whole hill out of it.

title: How — and why — to tell your doctor you’re feeling depressed
excerpt: Regularly talking to your provider about your mental health is the best way to get ahead of any problems and get treatment if you need it. | Paige Vickers/Vox;
body: Regularly talking to your provider about your mental health is the best way to get ahead of any problems and get treatment if you need it. | Paige Vickers/Vox; Getty Images I don’t know about you, but whenever I go to see my primary care doctor, my mental health isn’t usually at the top of my list of things to talk about
In fact, experts say that all of us could benefit from more candid conversations with our doctors about our mental health. (This story discusses mental health issues and suicide
If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available

You can call the national 988 hotline for support.) For years, the United States has been trying to figure out “parity” for mental health care — to have it treated and paid for like any other medical need, not something that is carved out and separate

A big part of that has been pushing primary care doctors and OB/GYNs to do more screenings, to make your mental state a part of your well-being that you discuss with your doctor the same as your blood pressure or any physical ailment
A lot of people may not even realize that their depression or anxiety or stress is something they should talk about with their primary care doctor
Others might fear being judged, and for good reason — national policymakers warn there continues to be a stigma toward mental health conditions among doctors

About one in three Americans say they have never been asked about their mental health by a doctor, which is unsettling considering that the nation has been going through a collective mental health crisis for several years
Men are significantly less likely to be asked about their mental health than women — perhaps a reflection of a culture that expects men to “tough it out” when it comes to their feelings
But those attitudes come with a price: Men are diagnosed with depression at half the rate as women , but die by suicide much more frequently
Much of the burden for starting these conversations should fall on your doctor to be more curious and accommodating during annual exams
But you don’t have to wait to be asked to bring it up
Regularly talking to your provider about your mental health is the best way to get ahead of any problems and get treated if you need to be

In honor of Suicide Prevention Month , I reached out to a handful of doctors who have studied why it’s sometimes so hard for patients and doctors to talk about depression, anxiety, and stress — and learned some novel strategies for how you can take charge, push through any stigma, and start having more honest talks with your doctor about your state of mind

Know the relevant symptoms before you talk to your doctor One of the tricky things about depression or any serious mental health problem is that it isn’t always easy to identify when you’re the one experiencing it. “Patients need to recognize their distress…as potentially emanating from depression,” Dr
Richard Kravitz , a general medicine professor at UC Davis who has studied depression screening in primary care, told me
There is a checklist of sorts that you can go through on your own to understand whether you’re just having a tough couple of days or there’s something more serious at work, said Dr
Maria Garcia , an internal medicine physician at UC San Francisco
You might be feeling down or unmotivated or have a lack of energy, or be more agitated, angry, or irritable than usual
Sometimes there are less obvious signs, like trouble with money or problems at work.  Symptoms of depression Here are some of the possible signs of depression, according to the Mayo Clinic
If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available
You can call the national 988 hotline for support

Feeling sad or hopeless or like you are a burden to others Feeling more irritable and angry than usual, losing your temper more easily Losing interest in most or all normal day-to-day activities and hobbies Sleep problems, whether you are sleeping too little or too much Feeling less energetic than usual Changes in appetite — whether you are eating less and losing weight or eating more and gaining weight Concentration and memory problems Unexplained physical symptoms “If you’re not getting enjoyment from your normal hobbies or talking to the people that you would normally really enjoy talking to, if you find yourself isolating from people that you normally really enjoy spending time with, I think those are certainly triggers,” she said

Consider the duration of your symptoms, too: “If it’s every day for a couple of weeks, that definitely isn’t normal.” And oftentimes, depression symptoms can mirror symptoms of other ailments or problems, like a lack of sleep, low appetite, or physical aches and pains
This is one reason why it is so important to talk with your doctor about it, Garcia said
Is that fatigue a result of depression — or is it a problem with your thyroid? Your primary care physician is best positioned to help you figure that out
One of the benefits of a long-term relationship with a physician is that they may be able to help you recognize symptoms of depression even if they aren’t obvious to you
It’s hard to be that self-aware; I’m certainly not all the time
But the more you pay attention to your mood and how it’s affecting your life, the more you can tell your doctor about what’s really going on

You don’t have to know all the fancy clinical terms, said Paul Duberstein , a clinical psychologist and professor of health behavior, society, and policy at the Rutgers School of Public Health. “The language that people are most comfortable using are words like stress or frustrated or impatient or something like that,” Duberstein told me. “Those are the kinds of things we really do want to incentivize and encourage people to talk to their doctors about.” How to bring up your mental health with your doctor Okay, you feel like something might be off and you have a doctor’s appointment coming up
What do you do? You might not have to do anything
These days, you are likely to be given a depression screening by your physician’s office before you ever arrive (usually as part of your pre-visit paperwork)
Garcia said it’s important to be honest and to be thorough when answering those questions, as that will tell your doctor that your mental health should be a focus for your upcoming visit
Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems

How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent  Dylan Scott  has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American healthcare policy

But if you aren’t proactively screened for depression and you have some of the symptoms described above or you just have a hunch that something might be wrong, try to alert your doctor in advance that your mental health is something you want to talk about
If that’s not possible, tell your doctor early on in the appointment that your mental state is something you want to discuss

Garcia said that, rightly or wrongly, doctors can sometimes be reluctant to dive deep into a discussion about mental health late into a visit; they only have so much time with individual patients, and they might balk at trying to squeeze in a mental health discussion at the end

The conversation is more likely to be productive if you proactively start it before your physician is sidetracked with your blood sugar.  During this conversation, you can ask for a depression screening outright
Doctors have become adept at recognizing code words; if you say your mood has been off, they may pick up the signal that you may be experiencing mental health struggles

title: The Supreme Court just handed Republicans a surprisingly decisive midterm loss
excerpt: Justice Elena Kagan, laughing | Doug Mills/Getty Images Wow, that was quick
body: Justice Elena Kagan, laughing | Doug Mills/Getty Images Wow, that was quick
At 10:03 am ET , according to the Supreme Court’s docket, a group of Republican plaintiffs filed a brief asking the Court to bless a GOP gerrymander in Missouri

Less than half an hour later, the Court issued a brief order telling these Republicans no — a rare scolding from this Court for the Republican Party, and a rejection of the party’s latest effort to skew elections in its favor
The decision is notable for this Court, but it isn’t particularly surprising
Earlier this week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied a similar request from another set of Republican litigants
But, minutes after Kavanaugh did so, a Donald Trump-appointed federal judge issued a new order that would have forced Missouri to use the Republican Party’s maps anyway
The Court’s new decision in People Not Politicians v
Onder places that judge’s decision on hold

As a practical matter, this means that, in the upcoming midterm elections, Missouri will almost certainly use the same maps it used in the 2024 election — which elected six Republicans and two Democrats to the US House — rather than the new maps, which were designed to give Republicans an extra seat.  Reading between the lines of the Court’s order in People Not Politicians , it appears that the justices were quite frustrated by the Republican Party’s tactics in this dispute

When Kavanaugh previously denied the GOP’s request to use its new gerrymandered maps, he did so using a process that allows a single justice to dispose of a case — a process the justices rarely use unless they view a matter as so one-sided that it’s not worth formally involving their colleagues

Similarly, the Court’s new order was issued almost immediately after the Republican plaintiffs filed their brief — so fast, in fact, that it’s unclear whether the justices even had time to read that brief
And the order also appears to be unanimous
No justice indicated that they dissent (although it is possible that one or more justices disagree with the order but decided not to make that disagreement public)
This is how the Court behaves when they want to send a clear signal that a litigant’s arguments are entirely without merit
It’s the judicial equivalent of a spanking

More broadly, the litigation over the Missouri gerrymander should give some assurance to Democrats, and to supporters of liberal democracy more broadly, that this Court isn’t wholly subservient to President Donald Trump or his Republican Party

The Court has a 6-3 Republican majority, and it often hands down decisions benefiting the GOP that cannot be defended using the traditional tools of legal reasoning — such as its 2024 decision holding that Trump may use the powers of the presidency to commit crimes
But it appears that there are some lines that this Court won’t allow the Republican Party to cross

Republicans created a “disaster” in Missouri and then demanded that the Supreme Court fix it It is likely that the Supreme Court’s decision in People Not Politicians will lead to some serious short-term chaos in Missouri, although all of that chaos should be blamed on Republican officials within Missouri

In September of 2025, the state’s Republican legislature enacted the new maps, as part of a broader Republican Party effort to gerrymander red states in order to give the GOP an edge in the upcoming midterm elections

But Missouri’s constitution permits opponents of a new law to put the law on hold if they collect enough signatures to trigger a ballot referendum — if a referendum is triggered, the state constitution provides that the law will not take effect unless it is approved by voters in the next election

Opponents of the new maps submitted their petitions seeking a referendum in December of 2025, but Missouri’s Republican secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, sat on those petitions for months — and then rejected them on the last possible date permitted under state law, August 4, 2026
As it happens, this was the same date that Missouri held its congressional primaries
So one consequence of Hoskins’s delay tactic is that many voters who voted in one district during the primary will vote in a different district in this November’s general election

Hoskins was able to delay litigation over whether the petitions seeking a referendum are valid because a state law provides that lawsuits concerning such a referendum must be filed within 10 days after the secretary of state rules on whether a referendum should take place
In any event, because of Hoskins’s delay, the Missouri Supreme Court did not rule on the referendum until September 3 , when it determined that Hoskins was wrong to reject the petitions

That means that the law enacting the new maps is not in effect and Missouri must use its old maps in the 2026 general election — even though that means that election officials must scramble to sort voters into their proper districts before November

In an extraordinary act of chutzpah, Hoskins argued in both the Missouri Supreme Court and the US Supreme Court that the state court’s decision came too late and should not take effect because reimplementing the old maps would be too disruptive

He even told the federal justices that “ a federal-election disaster is unfolding in Missouri .”  But, as the state supreme court said in its opinion, this argument is “particularly misplaced given the secretary’s delay created the confusion, expense, and practical difficulties of which he complains.” Given this background, the most surprising part of this case may be that a federal district judge then attempted to put the new maps in place, despite Hoskins’s tactics and despite the fact that Kavanaugh had already ruled against Missouri Republicans once

The Supreme Court’s new order technically only puts that district judge’s decision on temporary hold , but the hold should last through the 2026 election — thus ensuring that the old maps will be used in that election
The GOP’s legal arguments in People Not Politicians were weak Setting aside Hoskins’s bad behavior, Republicans made very similar arguments in both Hoskins and Onder , and those arguments were weak

I lay those arguments out in more detail here , but the short version is that they asked the Supreme Court to revive a discredited doctrine that it has rejected many times over the course of more than a century
And they also asked the justices to create a new right to vote in the same congressional district during both a primary and general election
In light of the Court’s new order in People Not Politicians , it appears that none of these arguments persuaded the justices
Again, that’s a reassuring sign for Democrats that this Court will not give Republicans literally anything that they ask for in an election-related case

Although it remains to be seen how the Court will rule on several other major election cases that are currently pending before the justices, including one that could potentially shut down voting by mail in many US states .

title: An elegant fix for one of America’s deadliest road problems
excerpt: When the Wallis-Annenberg Wildlife Crossing opens in December, it will be the largest of its kind in the world. | Dean Musgrove/Los Angeles Daily News In 2012,
body: When the Wallis-Annenberg Wildlife Crossing opens in December, it will be the largest of its kind in the world. | Dean Musgrove/Los Angeles Daily News In 2012, Southern California was besotted with an unlikely celebrity: a telegenic mountain lion who had crossed one of the state’s most perilous freeways , seeking a territory to call his own

Widely deemed “ LA’s loneliest lion ” and “ most eligible bachelor ,” the chiseled puma in question, named P-22, roamed the bustling but otherwise big cat-less Hollywood Hills, unable to safely return to the home he’d left behind

His search for a mate below the Hollywood Sign rendered him an icon of his city, but also a rueful reminder of the sprawling highways that bifurcated his habitat in the first place, leaving his clan on the other side of I-405 on the verge of local extinction .  Beth Pratt, then recently named head of California’s branch of the National Wildlife Federation, remembers strolling through Griffith Park with the wildlife biologist Jeff Sikich in 2012

Pratt knew that P-22 roamed somewhere nearby, and she found herself wondering aloud how she could help. “Well, there’s this little wildlife corridor we need to get built,” Sikich told her.  “I’m like, ‘Sure, how hard can it be?’” she recalled to me with a laugh. “Well, apparently, it’s quite hard.” Fourteen years later, the project they discussed that day, now known as the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, is finally scheduled to open in December

When it does, it will be the largest real-life animal crossing in the world, a gorgeous, vegetated overpass offering safe passage to local mountain lions, coyotes, deer, and black bears across the perilous 10-lane Ventura Freeway, where P-22 dodged cars back in 2012.  Though P-22 died before he could take advantage of that crossing himself, he helped engender a movement that, hard as it may have been to pull off in LA, could help revolutionize how animals cross America’s most dangerous roads, preventing some of the hundreds of human deaths , hundreds of millions of animal deaths , and billions in damages caused by wildlife collisions each year.  It is a species of elegant, bipartisan infrastructure that, if you squint, might even make you believe in America’s ability to build again, and to build in a way that still lends a hand — a paw, if you will — to the least empowered among us, a stranded salamander or the loneliest of lions.  As Pratt put it: “What’s more hopeful than rewilding one of the world’s busiest freeways?” Wildlife crossings used to be rare in the US
When Pratt first pitched the idea for a wildlife crossing across the 101, such projects were still rare in the US, and rarer still across such a major thoroughfare
As she recalls it, California’s transportation agency initially reacted with bafflement when she put the idea forward, a sign of just how novel the project was at the time
That made the process of getting it built more grueling than it needed to be, and likely more expensive, with a final price tag of over $100 million

But as LA meandered in its quest to build its unprecedented 210-feet-long Wallis Annenberg — beset, Pratt told me, by its complex engineering mandate, a funding model that relied on philanthropy, and the rising costs associated with construction and extreme weather — the rest of the nation took notice

In the 14 years since P-22 first crossed the 101 and the 405, over 1,000 new wildlife corridors have sprouted up across the country, a trend that culminated with the $350 million Wildlife Crossings Pilot Program , created in 2021 as part of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act

Many of these projects were championed by Pete Buttigieg, who was Transportation secretary under the Biden administration, and who told Vox last year that such passages are “not ornamental,” but rather “something that ties into the very core of our mission, which is to secure the safety of the American traveling public.” America’s burst of new wildlife corridors include a camouflaged overpass for elk crossing Interstate 25 in Colorado; a lush shared land bridge for deer, bobcats, and people passing over a Texan parkway; crossings for alligators passing under I-75 in the Florida everglades; and tiny tunnels under the Atlantic City expressway in New Jersey for migrating toadlets

California’s transportation agency, for its part, now boasts a division explicitly dedicated to building wildlife crossings, though many projects need not be as ambitious as the Wallis Annenberg. “Sometimes it’s pretty simple,” like a small hole to let hedgehogs through your fencing or a buzz stop for bees and butterflies crossing your lawn, Pratt said. “Sometimes it’s in your own backyard.” Along the way, a new set of norms have begun settling in at transportation agencies across the country, said Marcel Huijser, a research ecologist at the Western Transportation Institute, who noted that while “road ecology has become more recognized” in the US, the nation still has a very long way to go
Huijser is from the Netherlands, where wildlife crossings have been the norm for decades

The country boasts thousands of them in an area roughly double that of Massachusetts. “Most other parts of the world have done a better job at taking social and ecological impacts into consideration from the earliest decision processes onwards,” he told me, rather than “making it an afterthought.” And given that highways are already three times more expensive to build and maintain per mile in the US than they are elsewhere, it’s not the cost of conservation alone that has long kept the nation from incorporating such concerns into its road planning

Instead, as Huijser put it, “the norms, the values, [and] the culture” of the country have, until recently, ensured that planners rarely baked ecological considerations into the way it imagines its roadways
Wildlife advocates have instead been forced to rely, as activists in the US so often must, on a hodgepodge of lawsuits and local lobbying

The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing could well be transformative for local wildlife, and help keep Angelenos safer on the road for generations, but its most promising legacy may in fact be how it helped inspire a much broader movement and tranche of funding

The pilot program that P-22 helped inspire is now up for renewal, and seems poised to become permanent by the time that the Wallis Annenberg crossing opens in December.  Few wildlife corridors in the US will benefit from an über famous spokes-cat like P-22, a tireless local advocate like Pratt, or a roster of movie stars and philanthropists willing to pour time and money into building a new kind of bridge
Keeping local and federal governments on board with the projects may also be an uphill battle, given the national tenor

While many wildlife crossings have been embraced on a bipartisan basis, just a few months ago, Pratt received death threats after a smattering of right-wing media outlets assailed the Wallis Annenberg as a “butterfly bridge” to nowhere

A celebration of life for P-22 in Los Angeles. | David McNew/Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="David McNew/Getty Images" /> But if the US can successfully channel that cougar’s enduring star power into sustained support for a smart newish-to-us kind of infrastructure, one that’s been consistently shown to make a road much safer — and ultimately, cheaper ! — for humans and animals alike, then maybe there’s a fair chance for the rest of us, and maybe this stubborn nation can get better at building things more like it.  “These things should just be part of transportation budgets and embedded in our infrastructure planning,” said Pratt, who is planning her first vacation in seven years once the bridge finally opens in December. “The ultimate goal is you don’t need someone like me.”

title: Is it harder to have kids today? Or is it harder to want to?
excerpt: Anna Louie Sussman’s book, Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty, arrived as Rep
body: Anna Louie Sussman’s book, Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty, arrived as Rep

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been documenting her egg freezing journey. | Sarah Rice/Getty Images “From the outset, reproduction is a collaborative venture,” writes Anna Louie Sussman, a journalist who has spent years reporting how people all over the world try, and too often fail, to build the families they want

Her work explores how the collaborators of reproduction keep multiplying: doctors, employers, legislators, insurers, and a fertility industry that increasingly promises not just a baby but a better one.  In her new book, Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty , Sussman traces the economic, political, and psychological negotiations that stand between people and the children they say they want
Her reporting challenges the assumption that falling birth rates can be fully explained by metrics like income, marriage and education that demographers tend to focus on

She argues the answers are much more personal and resistant to measurement.  I wanted to better understand what Sussman meant by this idea of “impossibility of family” — and how one would even determine that, whether as a prospective parent or as a policymaker

What are the biggest barriers to having kids and how do people tell the difference between what they can’t afford and what they’ve come to believe they need? How much does the media conversation about these issues inform people’s choices?  I spoke with her about what Rep

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s egg freezing reveals about women who aren’t running for president, what countries that subsidize fertility treatment tell us about the demand going unmet here, and why she hesitates to say outright that having children is good
Our conversation has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity
You started working on this book seven years ago

What has most surprised you about how the conversation around fertility and family formation has changed in that time?  There are some people on the left who have always paid attention to family issues, like Elizabeth Warren with her work on bankruptcy and the “two-income trap,” but I do think we’ve been seeing a lot more movement there, with groups like the Congressional Dads Caucus [in 2023] , and care infrastructure ideas like those in the Build Back Better Act

There’s also been all this movement around paid leave in the states, 3-K and pre-K, and attempts for more affordable child care .  On the right there’s been the rise of this strange pronatalism and the turn that’s taken with what I’ve wound up calling “ kid-maxxing .” Plus this embrace in Silicon Valley and among the super rich with so-called super babies and the really overt embrace of technology to make children on this industrial scale
I also did not expect Roe to be overturned
I would have hoped that would’ve come with a lot more attention on the right to support for mothers and children, but that really hasn’t come to pass in a big way

I was startled to read that you found some philosophers attempting to reclaim the term “eugenics.” You cite one who wrote a paper called “ Defending eugenics ,” which sets out to “reclaim the spirit” of eugenicists like Charles Darwin and Francis Galton
You cite another who calls for “liberal eugenics” grounded in the freedom of parents to choose how to enhance their children in accordance with their own values
One Oxford philosopher even says parents have a duty of “ procreative beneficence ” and should select embryos or fetuses “most likely to have the best life” based on the genetic information they have
Like you, I also thought it was a discredited and taboo word
It’s hard to know how widespread those views are
I mean to be clear, eugenics has always been part of our culture in the US
I think people forget that a lot of Nazi policy was inspired by American eugenic policies , and it’s an attitude that has never really gone away
We still see it in a lot of subtler forms that I mention in the book

I mean, even just how people are choosing embryos and terminating pregnancies based on certain genetic conditions.  “Clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible.” This eugenicist rhetoric is gaining steam at a moment when some people are also really hard at work on developing technologies that could enable this sort of thing

While some of these philosophers will definitely make a distinction between parents making some individual choices vs. a state sponsored program, I think it’s the attitude that’s at the root of this, and that’s what we really need to work on criticizing and dismantling
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been documenting her egg freezing journey , and talking about how she wants to push to expand insurance coverage and federal support for fertility treatments

What does her experience — and the reaction to it — say about our current moment? Some on the right were so mad, as if she should just throw in the towel or eschew hope and agency at age 36.  What’s so interesting about her experience that I think that people miss is, yes, is it exceptional that she’s contemplating a run for president? Sure
But on many other levels, she’s doing what a lot of women who can afford to do in their late 30s do when they’re still single
In the book I mention the research of Marcia Inhorn , who interviewed about 150 women who sought to freeze their eggs
And what’s interesting is if you look at their profiles, they were city-dwelling professionals who were on average nearly 37 at the time of freezing

That is AOC to a tee, and if you asked those study participants why they were doing it, most were not doing so because they felt like they needed to put their families on hold to pursue careers. A full 82 percent cited their lack of a partner as the prime motivation

They wanted to have a family at some point and didn’t want to rule that out.  What do you think we should take from other countries that do subsidize egg freezing? So the city of Tokyo has subsidized egg freezing and they were totally oversubscribed
So many women took up the city’s offer, and France has also started offering it
More places offer IVF coverage for people who need it because they treat infertility like a disease, which is how the World Health Organization defines it
What’s interesting is when you look at places where there is more coverage, it also gives you a sense of the scale of need for it

So in Denmark, where you can get something like up to six rounds of treatment publicly funded for your first child and another six rounds for your second child; I believe about one in nine children is born there with assisted reproductive technologies
If you compare that with the US, it’s closer to one in 36
So clearly you could have a lot more children being born if these technologies were more accessible

In the book you cite historian Sara Matthiesen , who argues that since legal abortion helped transform having a child into more of a personal choice, pregnancy thus became understood as chosen, with parents then sacrificing or forfeiting some of their claim on societal help
I couldn’t tell where you landed on that argument
Do you find it persuasive? So I find it persuasive in the sense that I feel like conservatives will grab onto any argument to avoid state responsibility towards families and children

The fact that you can terminate a pregnancy is one more reason that can be provided to individualize the responsibility of parenthood.  But I think that we’re also seeing the mirror image of that — where the choice to remain or not remain pregnant has also been taken away in so many places post- Roe

title: A grim report card for the world’s schools
excerpt: A student takes the French general baccalaureate exam on June 15, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained,&nbs
body: A student takes the French general baccalaureate exam on June 15, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
A growing chorus of teachers, parents, and education experts is worried that American students can’t read

But, hear me out, silver lining here: At least the students are in good company . (Okay, maybe that’s not exactly a silver lining.) A new report from the Programme for International Student Assessment, or PISA — a standardized global test of 15-year-olds’ math, reading, and science skills, administered by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — finds that scores in all three subjects have dipped to their lowest levels in OECD countries since testing began in the early 2000s
Reading scores fell especially sharply, by the equivalent of more than a year of education, between 2015 and 2025

In the US, reading scores fell by roughly 14 percentage points between 2022 and 2025.  These results, based on a sample of more than 760,000 students from 91 countries, are among the most-watched educational metrics in the world

And the million-dollar question — as always — is why those metrics continue to fall.  The report gestures at the usual suspects: the lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic; an attentional crisis that makes it difficult for kids ( and adults! ) to stick with long texts.  PISA also surveyed students about their use of generative AI, the first time it’s done so since the technology became widely available
But as I’ll explain more below, anyone looking for clear takeaways on classroom AI and its effect on learning will probably be disappointed
Go a little deeper View Link If you know a high school student, chances are they use AI for school
In the PISA report, 86 percent said they use it at least occasionally, and roughly one in 10 use it every day
But whether that helps or hurts learning seems to depend on how students use it
In this report, the small minority of students who never use AI generally outperformed those who do
But weekly users who used AI to “help them learn,” as opposed to using it to complete specific tasks, performed about as well as nonusers
And frequent AI users who were also taught AI literacy skills scored slightly higher

In other words, the unsatisfying answer to the question “Is AI good or bad for learning?” is probably…“it depends.” My colleague Adam Clark Estes took on this question last year, and found several promising applications of the technology in education: tools that free teachers from grunt work, for instance, and educational chatbots designed to provide personalized tutoring.  In upstate New York, where I’m based, a federally funded research center is developing AI tools for children with learning and language disorders
One mother told me she credited an AI reading app with dramatically improving her autistic son’s communication.  That nuance complicates the policy discussion around AI and education

Some of these applications would likely be disallowed under New York City’s new, one-year AI moratorium , for instance, which bans student-facing generative AI tools in public elementary and middle schools in the country’s largest district
In announcing the ban, schools chancellor Kamar Samuels argued a pause would allow the district to evaluate which tools, and which use cases, truly help students learn

That’s the assignment now facing educators and policymakers the world over — presumably, they won’t ask ChatGPT to do it for them.  One link for later ➨ Fight for your right to leave your phone at home
An ever-larger range of everyday tasks now requires a smartphone : reading a menu, parking a car, taking public transit, etc
But while the QR-codification of daily life can sometimes be convenient, it also locks many elderly and low-income people out of services and locks the rest of us into a cycle of digital dependence

Or consumer resistance.  Before you go… Did you know… that almost all of America’s walkable urban neighborhoods date back to before World War II ? In other words, you can live in a new house or apartment, or you can live in a walkable place

But most people won’t have the option to do both until the US builds denser urban housing.  Today’s trivia: In Greek and Roman mythology, who was the legendary founder and first queen of Carthage? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the archipelago that includes the Isle of Skye

That would be the Inner Hebrides, off the coast of Scotland, whose landscapes have inspired a wide range of cultural works: among them, the Enya song “ Ebudæ ,” the original screenplay for Peter Pan , and George Orwell’s 1984 .

body: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week
The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period
In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas
A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people
Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region
More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas
At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes
On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing
